title: Design notes
text: SymJ is a symbolic manipulation kernel written in pure Julia. It aims for SymEngine-class speed with a small, explicit core that later layers (simplification, solving, matrices) build on.

title: Goals
text: Speed comparable to SymEngine. Construction, canonicalization, expansion, differentiation and substitution should be within a small factor of SymEngine, and ideally faster.Callable objects. Symbolic objects subtype Function (via AbstractSymbolic). Calling is meant to make expressions drop-in …

title: Implementation
text: This page discusses the main design choices in SymJ and the reasons for them. The Design notes record each decision in more detail, with measurements. SymJ set out to be a symbolic kernel in pure Julia with the speed of SymEngine, exact numbers, and expressions that behave like functions. Most of …

title: One concrete node type
text:
Every expression is a Sym, a single concrete type with a kind tag (number, symbol, constant, sum, product, power, function application). This is SymEngine's approach, and differs from a Julia type per kind of node: mutable struct Sym <: AbstractSymbolic
    const kind::Kind              # NUMBER …

title: Canonical form as you go
text: Sums collect like terms and products collect like bases when they are built: x + 2x is 3x, x*y*x is x^2*y, exp(x)*exp(y) is exp(x + y). There is no separate simplification pass for these identities, so a - a == 0 holds for any a. A sum is stored as a constant plus sorted parallel vectors of terms …

title: Exact numbers
text: Numbers are SymNumber, which holds a small rational in two Ints, a Rational{BigInt}, or a Float64. The fast path. Arithmetic on small values uses Int with overflow checks. On overflow it moves to BigInt, and back when a result fits again. Most coefficient arithmetic never allocates.Exactness. No …

title: Expressions as functions
text: Sym is a subtype of Function. The goal is for expressions to be drop-in replacements for functions in numeric code: Calling with a number evaluates with Julia's arithmetic on that number: if u = x^2, then u(3) === 9, u(3.0) === 9.0 and u(1//2) === 1//4. Because this is generic, dual numbers …

title: Polynomials
text: Polynomial algorithms (expansion, division, gcd, factoring, partial fractions, solving) run on a separate type, Poly{C,M}, a sparse multivariate polynomial: a vector of generators, sorted vectors of monomials and coefficients, and a description of how exponents are packed.

title: Packed monomials
text: A monomial's exponents are packed into one machine word, with the first generator in the most significant bits. For x^3*y^2 in two generators with 32-bit fields, the word is 3 << 32 + 2. Then: multiplying monomials is adding words (degree checks rule out carries);lexicographic order is integer …

title: When the exponents don't fit
text: The usual packing gives each of n generators 64 ÷ n bits: 4 generators allow degree 65 534 each, and 16 allow 14. Exponents that don't fit are handled in two stages: Uneven fields. The fields are sized to each generator's degree, with the spare bits shared out. One generator of high degree among …

title: Division
text: Multivariate division keeps the dividend in the same hash table used for products, with a heap of its monomials. Each step takes the largest monomial; everything added to the table is smaller, so no monomial is revisited and the quotient and remainder come out already sorted, without forming …

title: Greatest common divisors
text: Polynomial gcds are at the heart of rational function arithmetic (cancel), squarefree and full factorization, partial fractions and solving, so their speed sets the speed of much else.

title: Why a modular algorithm
text: The classical method is a sequence of pseudo-remainders, made primitive at each step. Its coefficients grow quickly, and it is very slow beyond small inputs: 720 ms for a 4-variable gcd that the modular method does in 1.9 ms. SymJ keeps it only as a reference implementation for the tests, and for …

title: Sparse gcds: Zippel's method
text: Brown's method interpolates every possible term, so its cost is exponential in the number of variables, whatever the size of the answer. A gcd of 14 low-degree variables took 1.1 s, and 18 variables more than a minute. Zippel's method learns the gcd's terms from one image and then solves only for …

title: Factorization
text: Factoring over the rationals starts with the squarefree decomposition, by Yun's algorithm: a few gcds with a derivative separate the factors by multiplicity, and each squarefree part is then factored into irreducibles. Univariate polynomials use the Zassenhaus approach: factor modulo a small prime …

text: cancel brings an expression to the form p/q in lowest terms. Its polynomial variables are the expression's atoms: symbols, but also function applications and non-integer powers. Treating sin(x) as an independent variable is always sound, since a polynomial identity in it remains true after …

The left side minus the right is reduced with cancel, so no root is a pole, and the numerator is factored. Each …

text: When a symbolic value meets a Julia integer or rational, the number becomes an exact symbolic number: 2x, x / 3, (1 // 2) * x(2*x, x/3, x/2)  Sym makes an exact number directly. Exact numbers keep radicals and π exact, and simplify standard values: Sym(1 // 3), sqrt(Sym(8)), cos(Sym(π) / 6), …

title: Watch out for early conversion
text: Julia evaluates 1/2 before SymJ sees it, giving the float 0.5. A float in an expression makes the result a float, so x * (1/2) is not x/2: x / 2 == x * (1 // 2), x / 2 == x * (1 / 2)(true, false)  The same holds for sqrt(2) or pi * 2 evaluated before meeting a symbol. Since an expression in one variable is callable, it can be passed where a function is expected, for instance to a plotting package: using Plots
plot(sin(x)^2 * exp(-x / 4), 0, 4pi)

title: Construction
text:
A polynomial expression can be expanded with expand: p = expand((x - 1) * (x - 2) * (x + 3))x^3 - 7*x + 6  Poly converts an expression into a polynomial in given generators. Its coefficients and exponents are available, and Sym converts it back: P = Poly(p, x)
coefficients(P), exponent_vectors(P), …

title: Evaluation and shifts
text: A polynomial is evaluated by calling it; a shift is a substitution: p(2), expand(p(x => x + 1))(0, x^3 + 3*x^2 - 4*x)

title: Factoring
text: factor factors over the rationals, in any number of variables: factor(p), factor(x^4 + 4), factor(x^6 - y^6)((x + 3)*(x - 1)*(x - 2), (x^2 + 2*x + 2)*(x^2 - 2*x + 2), (-x*y + x^2 + y^2)*(x + y)*(x - y)*(x*y + x^2 + y^2))  factor_squarefree only separates repeated factors, which is cheaper: …

title: Roots
text:
solve finds the roots of a polynomial. Degrees up to four are solved exactly, with real roots of cubics given in trigonometric form (no complex numbers needed): solve(p ~ 0, x)3-element Vector{Sym}:
 -3
 1
 2  solve(x^3 - 3x + 1 ~ 0, x)3-element Vector{Sym}:
 2*cos(10*π/9)
 2*cos(4*π/9)
 …

title: Rational functions
text:
cancel reduces a rational expression to lowest terms: r = (x^3 - 1) / (x^2 - 1)
cancel(r)(x^2 + x + 1)/(x + 1)  cancel(1 / x + 1 / (x + 1))(2*x + 1)/(x^2 + x)  numer_denom gives the numerator and denominator without reducing: numer_denom(r)(x^3 - 1, x^2 - 1)

title: Partial fractions
text: apart decomposes a rational function into a polynomial part and simple fractions: apart((x^3 + 1) / (x^2 - 1), x)x + 1/(x - 1)  apart(1 / (x^4 - 1), x)-1/(4*(x + 1)) + 1/(4*(x - 1)) - 1/(2*(x^2 + 1))  Other symbols are allowed in the coefficients: apart(1 / ((x - a) * (x - b)), x)-1/((-a + b)*(-a + …

title: Solving equations
text:
An equation is written with ~, which binds more loosely than everything else, so no parentheses are needed: solve(x^2 + 2x ~ 3, x)2-element Vector{Sym}:
 -3
 1  Equations in which x appears through one function are solved by solving for that function first: solve(exp(2x) - 3exp(x) + 2 ~ 0, …

title: Inequalities
text: < and its relatives compare numbers and return true or false, so inequalities use other operators: ≪ (typed \ll), ≦ (\leqq), ≫ (\gg), ≧ (\geqq) and ≶ (\lessgtr). The solution is a union of intervals: solve(x^2 - 1 ≫ 0, x)(-∞, -1) ∪ (1, ∞)  solve((x - 1) / (x + 2) ≧ 0, x)(-∞, -2) ∪ [1, ∞)

title: Systems
text:
A list of linear equations in several unknowns gives a Dict: solve([x + y ~ 3, x - y ~ 1], [x, y])Dict{Sym, Sym} with 2 entries:
  y => 1
  x => 2  solve([a * x + y ~ 1, x - y ~ b], [x, y])Dict{Sym, Sym} with 2 entries:
  y => (-a*b + 1)/(a + 1)
  x => (b + 1)/(a + 1)  A system of linear …

title: Limits
text: Limits are computed by limit from GruntzLimit, which implements Gruntz's algorithm. limit(f, x => x0) is the limit of f as x tends to x0, a number, an expression or Inf: limit(sin(x) / x, x => 0)1  limit((1 + 1 / x)^x, x => Inf), limit(x * ((1 + 1 / x)^x - ℯ), x => Inf)(ℯ, -ℯ/2)  …

title: Derivatives
text: diff(f, x) differentiates with respect to x, and diff(f, x, n) gives the n-th derivative: diff(sin(x)^2 * exp(x), x)2*cos(x)*sin(x)*exp(x) + sin(x)^2*exp(x)  diff(x^x, x), diff(atan(x), x, 3)((log(x) + 1)*x^x, -2/(x^2 + 1)^2 + 8*x^2/(x^2 + 1)^3)  Mixed partial derivatives take the variables in …

title: Critical points
text:
The critical points of a function are the zeros of its derivative, and the second derivative classifies them: h = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 1
cps = solve(diff(h, x) ~ 0, x)2-element Vector{Sym}:
 1
 3  h2 = diff(h, x, 2)
[(c, h(c), h2(c)) for c in cps]2-element Vector{Tuple{Sym, Sym, Sym}}:
 (1, 5, -6)
 …

title: Tangent lines
text:
The tangent line at c is h(c) + h'(c)(x - c): c₀ = 2
expand(h(c₀) + diff(h, x)(c₀) * (x - c₀))-3*x + 9

title: Series
text: series(ex, x, x0, n) expands ex about x0 with an error of order (x - x0)^n; x0 defaults to 0 and n to 6: series(sin(x), x)x - x^3/6 + x^5/120 + O(x^6)  series(exp(x), x, 1, 3)ℯ + ℯ*(x - 1) + ℯ/2*(x - 1)^2 + O((x - 1)^3)  Laurent series (negative powers), Puiseux series (fractional powers), …

title: Integrals
text: Antiderivatives come from integrate, from RischIntegrate, an implementation of the Risch algorithm. It decides whether an elementary antiderivative exists, and finds it: integrate(x^2 * exp(x), x)(x^2 - 2*x + 2)*exp(x)  integrate(1 / (x^3 + 1), x)log(x + 1)/3 - log(x^2 - x + 1)/6 + …

title: Definite integrals
text:
A definite integral is the difference of an antiderivative's values at the end points. Calling the antiderivative with exact numbers keeps the answer exact: F = integrate(x^2, x)
F(3) - F(0)9//1  G = integrate(sin(x), x)
G(x => Sym(π)) - G(x => 0)2

title: What SymJ does not do yet
text: Simplification under assumptions. Identities such as sqrt(x^2) = x for positive x need assumptions, which are not implemented.Matrices and noncommutative algebra.Nonlinear systems of equations, and equations in several unrelated functions of the unknown, such as sin(x) + cos(x) ~ 1.

title: SymJ
text: SymJ is under active development. Its interface may change, including in ways that break existing code, before a stable release. SymJ is a symbolic manipulation kernel written in pure Julia. It builds expressions in a canonical form as you go, keeps numbers exact, and is fast: construction, …

title: General usage
text: using SymJ

title: Symbolic variables and numbers
text:
Variables are made with @syms, or with Sym from a name. Numbers stay exact: Sym makes an exact number, and arithmetic with symbols keeps integers and rationals exact. @syms x y z
p = (x + 1)^2 / 3(x + 1)^2/3  sqrt(Sym(8)), sin(Sym(π) / 3), Sym(2)^100(2*sqrt(2), sqrt(3)/2, …

title: Expressions are built in canonical form
text: Sums collect like terms and products collect like bases as they are built, with no separate simplification step: x + 2x - y + x * y * x, exp(x) * exp(y), (x * y)^2(x^2*y + 3*x - y, exp(x + y), x^2*y^2)

title: Calling an expression
text:
An expression is a Function. Called with a number, it evaluates with Julia's own arithmetic, so it works in numeric code (with dual numbers, BigFloat, intervals, …): u = x^2 - 2x
u(3), u(3.0), u(1 // 2)(3, 3.0, -3//4)  Called with pairs, it substitutes; subs does the same: ex = x^2 * y + …

title: Equations and inequalities
text: An equation is written with ~; solve (from CommonSolve) finds its solutions. An inequality uses ≪ (typed \ll), ≦, ≫, ≧ or ≶, since < is kept for comparing numbers and returns a Bool. solve(x^2 - 5x + 6 ~ 0, x), solve(x^3 - 3x + 1 ~ 0, x)(Sym[2, 3], Sym[2*cos(10*π/9), 2*cos(4*π/9), …

title: Calculus
